title: A Spiral Galaxy “Oracle”: Prelude-and-Fugue No.7, Book I
content_blocks: Prelude-and-Fugue No.7 is unique in many ways. First, the minimalist prelude flows into and continues during the fugue, this is thus an accompanied fugue (where the fugal voices are accompanied by a separate, non-fugal voice). Also, this is a two-voice fugue, which is not only unique in Expanded Universe but is unusual in music history. At four full measures, the fugue subject is one of the longest in the set; by the time the answer enters the original voice weaves itself back into the minimalist accompaniment. These features reduce the fugal character of the piece, even despite the stretti in the second and third fugal sections.

The passages between the first and the second, and between the third and the fourth fugal sections introduce a leaping motive—reminiscent of the leaps in Prelude No.3. But it is in the brief passage between the second and third fugal sections that the most important (and unique) feature of this piece is revealed: the entire prelude-and-fugue is a retrograde inversion of itself. The “axis” of this retrograde inversion occurs at about 2’25” in Michael Mizrahi’s entrancing performance, with the repeated F#s. From there, the entire piece is repeated (upside down and backward); we learn that even the fugue subject is a retrograde inversion of itself.

Composers’ fascination with the idea of a spiral, where the music can be played upside down and backward, is not a new idea. Bach played with ‘cancrizans’—‘crab’—canons in The Musical Offering (Shunske Sato created two great videos showing one of Bach’s canons that do this, here and here; note the upside down and backward clef and flat sign in the score shown briefly at the beginning of the second video). These are sometimes called “canone al contrario riverso” in Latin, or “table canons,” since the music can be placed on a table and have the two performers read it simultaneously from opposite sides of the table. I wrote a piece called Spiral Galaxy which does much the same thing, in a piece for saxophone quartet (you can hear the two movements here and here, which also show some of my interest in birds and other wildlife).

Even the mode of this piece—a 9-note scale that repeats at the twelfth—is a retrograde inversion of itself.  It allows for an abundance of major or minor triads, giving it quite a consonant feel.  But it also allows for the retrograde inversion of the entire piece to sound identical to the untransformed version.  As with Prelude and Fugue No.13, the mode used in this piece is not used in any of the other pieces (#s 1 & 8,  2, 4, & 9, 3 & 10, 5 & 11, and 6 & 12 share their modes).

My character label for this prelude-and-fugue from four years ago was a choice between The Visionary and The Oracle. I’m pretty baffled by the first label (what was I thinking?!); I suppose that The Oracle makes sense if you think of an oracle as speaking in riddles that go around in circles. If you can guess what I was thinking back then, or if you would like to let me know if you have a better character label, please contact me!
Bach played with the idea of a spiral, where the music can be played upside down and backward, in The Musical Offering.
